transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Cleveland, Ohio, I'm Dale Willman.
A federal appeals court has rejected the Justice Department's request to set aside
thousands of California ballots, NPR's Jew Joffee Block reports.
In a two-to-one vote, a Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel rejected the
Trump administration's request.
The Justice Department wants California election officials to stop processing
ballots pertaining to 20,000 people, federal officials say, are likely
non-citizens.
But the accuracy of that list is in question.
The appeals court ruling upholds a federal court opinion from earlier this week.
The majority noted the Justice Department's last-minute request could
disenfranchise eligible voters and put the vote-counting process in jeopardy.
The same two judges had already ruled against the Justice Department earlier
in this case.
A third judge dissented. Jew Joffee Block, NPR News.
With just days left before the midterm elections, the Senate race in Alaska is in
turmoil.
The New York Times reported this week that Democratic operatives recruited a spoiler
candidate who shares the same name as the Republican candidate to run.
While the news is people talking throughout the state, Alaska Public Media's Liz
Ruskin says there appears to be nothing criminal about what happens.
Even though Governor Mike Dunlavy ordered a different state agency to investigate
whether the spoiler recruitment operation described in the Times broke any laws,
several legal experts I interviewed said they don't know of any legal violations
based on what they read in the Times.
In Alaska, a candidate's motives just don't matter legally.
That's reporter Liz Ruskin in Alaska.
France's Interior Minister is warning there's a very high risk of violence and
public disorder around protests planned for Saturday.
As NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports, the security presence will be massive.
70,000 police are expected on French streets, including elite units as well as
helicopters, drones, water cannon trucks, and armored vehicles.
The French nightly news is full of the kind of videos that worry the government.
Social media posts calling on young people to come out in costumes and masks
to party and some calling for chaos.
The confluence of Halloween with the protests has forced many cities to cancel
Halloween celebrations and ban the sale of fireworks.
In Paris, where more than 100,000 demonstrators are expected in the streets
Saturday, authorities are working to change the planned protest route to avoid
the city center.
Eleanor Beardsley in Pierre News, Paris.
It was a bad day on Wall Street Friday with stocks dropping over concerns that
the excitement over AI sent stocks too high.
The Nasdaq fell almost 3% after Intel saw its biggest loss since 1974.
The company released a profit forecast that fell below the expectation of analysts.
The S&P 500 finished the day down 1.8% while the Dow dropped 1.1%.
This is NPR News.
Pope Leo has cast a ballot in the U.S. election.
The Vatican confirmed that Leo voted in Chicago using an absentee ballot.
In a statement, the Vatican said the first U.S. pontiff has a strong belief in civic
participation.
Under U.S. law, citizens living abroad have the right to vote by using an absentee
ballot.
A federal judge is opening an inquiry into potential misconduct by Trump
administration officials in carrying out President Trump's plans to renovate a
historic public golf course in Washington, D.C.
NPR's Rachel Triesman reports.
Justice Department lawyers have repeatedly contradicted President Trump's
social media posts by telling District Judge Ana Reyes that there is no imminent
plan to close East Potomac for renovations in mid-November.
They changed course in court filings this week, prompting Reyes to order this
latest hearing.
Reyes grilled the government's lawyers about details of the plan, which they now
say will keep much of the riverfront park closed to repair its deteriorating
seawall.
Reyes closed the four-hour hearing by announcing an inquiry into officials'
conduct in the case, including whether they misrepresented the government's
plans for the municipal golf course.
She says she will select a special master to lead that investigation, or if the
government prefers, conduct it herself.
Rachel Triesman, NPR News.
More than 7,700,000 screaming fans greeted the Milwaukee Brewers Friday
during a parade in downtown Milwaukee.
They were celebrating the team's World Series title, the first in franchise
history. They beat the Tampa Bay Rays Wednesday 4-1 in Game 5.
The players were greeted by fans gathered at a downtown amphitheater lining
downtown streets and hanging out of office building windows to catch a glimpse
of the champions.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.

topics.text: Federal appeals court rejects Justice Department request to set aside thousands of California ballots
Alaska Senate race turmoil over reported spoiler candidate recruited by Democratic operatives, with no clear crime found
France braces for Saturday protests with 70,000 police deployed and Halloween events canceled
Wall Street stocks drop Friday as Intel posts steep loss and AI enthusiasm fades
Vatican confirms Pope Leo cast an absentee ballot in the U.S. election from Chicago
Federal judge Ana Reyes opens inquiry into Trump officials' conduct over East Potomac golf course renovations
Milwaukee Brewers celebrate first World Series title with downtown parade drawing huge crowds
